Ensembles of models

Source: R/model-ensemble.R
ensemble.Rd

A mixture (linear pool, Gneiting and Ranjan 2013) of the predictive distributions of several models: each draw of the ensemble is a draw of one component, chosen with the weights as probabilities. Mixing draws keeps the paths coherent, so derived quantities such as life expectancy can be computed from the ensemble draws.

Usage

ensemble(
  ...,
  weights = "equal",
  inner_origins = NULL,
  inner_h = NULL,
  top_k = NULL,
  inner_n_draws = 100
)

Arguments

...

Model specifications; names are used as labels.

weights

"equal", "crps_stack", "bias", "crps", the deprecated "stack", or a numeric vector.

inner_origins, inner_h

Inner backtest for the weights other than "equal" and numeric ones, and for top_k: the number of origins and the horizon of each inner forecast. The last origin is inner_h years before the last training year. Defaults: 3 origins and 5 years; with weights = "bias", one origin and 13 years (Kontis et al. 2017).

top_k

Keep only the top_k components with the lowest CRPS in the inner backtest on the training years (the others get weight 0); NULL keeps all.

inner_n_draws

Draws per inner forecast of the inner backtest.

Value

A model specification.

Details

Weights:

  • "equal" (default);

  • a numeric vector (normalised to sum to 1);

  • "crps_stack": stacking of predictive distributions (Yao, Vehtari, Simpson and Gelman 2018, Section 2.1, eq. 2.2): the weights on the simplex that optimise a proper scoring rule of the mixture, averaged over held-out predictions. The scoring rule is the CRPS. Yao et al. define stacking for any proper scoring rule (their Section 2.1 lists the CRPS among them) and use the logarithmic score, which needs predictive densities; the CRPS, which draws give directly, is a choice of this package. The CRPS is proper, and strictly proper for distributions with a finite mean (Gneiting and Raftery 2007, Section 4.2). The held-out predictions are the forecasts of the inner rolling-origin backtest on the training years (leave-future-out validation, as in Barigou et al. 2023) in place of the leave-one-out predictions of Yao et al.; they are scored on the observed log death rates, as in mt_backtest(). With draws X_k of component k, the CRPS of the mixture at an observation y is sum_k w_k E|X_k - y| - 1/2 sum_k sum_l w_k w_l E|X_k - X_l'| with X_k and X_l' independent (the kernel form of Gneiting and Raftery 2007, eq. 21, applied to the mixture). The expectations are means over all draws and all pairs of draws, so this is the CRPS of the pooled draws with weight w_k / n for each of the n draws of component k, the estimator of the backtest. Its mean over the scored cells is a quadratic function of the weights, convex on the simplex (the CRPS is the integral of a squared difference of distribution functions, Gneiting and Raftery 2007, eq. 20). The exact minimum of this quadratic program is found by an active-set method. Weights can be 0, and the minimum need not be unique (for example with identical components). Yao et al. (2018, Section 2.3) note that the weights can be unstable when the held-out sample is small; the cells of an inner backtest with few origins are correlated;

  • "bias": the weights of Kontis et al. (2017, Methods, "Bayesian model averaging", steps 1 to 3). They withhold the last 13 years of data, fit each model to the earlier years and project the withheld years. The projection bias of a model is the observed minus the projected life expectancy, averaged over the withheld years. A model gets the weight exp(-|bias|), and the weights are normalised to sum to 1. The final projections pool draws of the models fitted to all data in proportion to the weights. Here the withheld years are those of the inner backtest with one origin 13 years before the last training year (inner_origins = 1, inner_h = 13, the defaults with weights = "bias"). The projected life expectancy is that of the mean forecast rates in each age group and year, here the means of the predictive draws of the inner backtest (the code published with the paper uses the life expectancy of the posterior mean rates). The observed life expectancy is that of the observed rates. Both are computed by life_expectancy() in the observed age groups at the first age of the data, so at birth only when the data start at age 0 (the code published with the paper uses life expectancy at birth). Withheld years whose observed age groups do not cover the age range are skipped, as in mt_backtest(). Package-specific (reference unknown): with several strata, one weight per component from the mean over the strata of |bias| (the paper weights each country and sex separately; fit one ensemble per population with stratified() to do so); with inner_origins > 1, the mean of |bias| over the origins. The draws of the ensemble come from the components with the weights as probabilities; the paper takes numbers of draws proportional to the weights;

  • "crps": proportional to the inverse mean CRPS of each component in the inner backtest. Shang (2012, Section 3.2.1) weights point forecasts of age-specific life expectancies in inverse proportion to their mean absolute forecast errors in a validation period, following Bates and Granger (1969), and normalises the weights to sum to 1. He combines all models, or the two best ones, this way and compares these combinations with equal and Bayesian model averaging weights (Tables 18 and 19). The CRPS of a point forecast is its absolute error (Gneiting and Raftery 2007, Section 4.2), so the inverse mean CRPS extends these weights to predictive distributions. This extension, the log rates as the scored quantity and the use of the weights as mixture probabilities are package-specific. top_k = 2 keeps the two components with the lowest inner CRPS, as Shang's combination of the two best models;

  • "stack" (deprecated; use "crps_stack"): weights that minimise the squared error of the weighted mean of the components' median forecasts (log rates) in the same inner backtest, constrained to be non-negative and to sum to 1. This is stacking of point forecasts (Breiman 1996; for mortality, Kessy, Sherris, Villegas and Ziveyi 2022). Using these weights as the probabilities of the mixture is a deviation: they are optimal for the linear combination of the medians, not for the mixture distribution, whose median is not the weighted mean of the medians. It still works and warns (class mt_warning_deprecated).

Each draw of the ensemble comes from one component for all strata, so paths keep the dependence between strata and the coherence of reconciled components (reconciled()). A component that fails in a stratum is replaced there by the other components in proportion to their weights; this is recorded in the diagnostics. Any model specification can be a component, including joint models, Bayesian models, tuned, bootstrapped and reconciled models, and other ensembles. The components must forecast the same strata: with reconciled() components, add the aggregates of the hierarchy to the data first (mt_aggregate_strata()).

Weights from the inner backtest ("crps_stack", "bias", "crps", "stack", top_k) use only the training data, so they never use data after the forecast origin, also inside an outer backtest. They compare the components on the cells that all of them forecast. A component whose inner backtest fails gets weight 0; when every inner backtest fails, the weights are equal, with a warning of class mt_warning_ensemble_weights. With top_k, the stacking weights of "crps_stack" are computed among the kept components; with the other weights, the dropped components get weight 0.

A mixture is wider than its components when they disagree, which often corrects the too narrow intervals of single models; a linear pool of different calibrated components is overdispersed (Gneiting and Ranjan 2013). Its CRPS is never larger than the weighted mean of the CRPS of its components (the CRPS is convex in the forecast distribution). The vignette "Choosing and combining models" compares ensembles and single models in a backtest. In populations with few deaths per cell, the plain random walk accumulates the Poisson noise of observed rates and its long-horizon paths become implausible; the local level model with drift, the random walk observed with noise, is arima_series(order = c(0, 1, 1), drift = TRUE) (its reduced form, Harvey 1989).

References

Barigou K, Goffard P-O, Loisel S, Salhi Y (2023). Bayesian model averaging for mortality forecasting using leave-future-out validation. International Journal of Forecasting 39(2): 674-690. doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2022.01.011

Bates JM, Granger CWJ (1969). The combination of forecasts. Operational Research Quarterly 20(4): 451-468.

Breiman L (1996). Stacked regressions. Machine Learning 24(1): 49-64.

Gneiting T, Raftery AE (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477): 359-378. doi:10.1198/016214506000001437

Gneiting T, Ranjan R (2013). Combining predictive distributions. Electronic Journal of Statistics 7: 1747-1782.

Harvey AC (1989). Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter. Cambridge University Press.

Kessy SR, Sherris M, Villegas AM, Ziveyi J (2022). Mortality forecasting using stacked regression ensembles. Scandinavian Actuarial Journal 2022(7): 591-626.

Kontis V, Bennett JE, Mathers CD, Li G, Foreman K, Ezzati M (2017). Future life expectancy in 35 industrialised countries: projections with a Bayesian model ensemble. The Lancet 389(10076): 1323-1335. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(16)32381-9

Shang HL (2012). Point and interval forecasts of age-specific life expectancies: a model averaging approach. Demographic Research 27(21): 593-644. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2012.27.21

Yao Y, Vehtari A, Simpson D, Gelman A (2018). Using stacking to average Bayesian predictive distributions (with discussion). Bayesian Analysis 13(3): 917-1007. doi:10.1214/17-BA1091

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single")
ens <- ensemble(lc = lee_carter(), rw = rwd())
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(ens, x), h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
# \donttest{
# stacking weights from an inner backtest on the training years
st <- ensemble(lc = lee_carter(), rw = rwd(), weights = "crps_stack",
               inner_origins = 2, inner_h = 3)
mt_fit(st, x)$weights
#>         lc         rw 
#> 0.95400886 0.04599114 
# }
